messages.subject: Sampling Frequency
parts:
Hi all,

Has anyone checked the impacts of different sampling frequencies on final GGIR outcomes? 
If not, is there any way to resample data within the code? 

Kind regards

messages.author: 017566be30afa7f3
messages.subject: Re: [GGIR] Sampling Frequency
parts:
Hi Javad,

Good question. I am currently involved in a study that looks into this and we hope to submit our work to a journal this summer... so my hands are bit tight to answer this in detail. However, I can say the following:

GGIR has been designed to be minimally sensitive to sample frequency. For example, GGIR does not attempt to rely on specific very short lasting events or high frequency signal components. Also, GGIR intentionally does not attempt to detect patterns in the raw data.

The real problem, I think, is that a few accelerometer brands are poor at capturing the acceleration of movement consistently across sample frequency settings. Therefore, I think your question should be accelerometer brand specific.

You give the impression that resampling is a solution to a lack of comparability of raw data, but resampling itself can also introduce discrepancies and on top of that resampling does not address a systematic bias caused by sampling rate. For example, if X Hertz results in 10% lower magnitude of acceleration then resampling will not be able to fix that. A better solution would be to either identify the source of the bias and address it, or to identify problematic accelerometer brand and sample rate combinations and discourage their use.

Kind regards,

Vincent

messages.subject: Re: [GGIR] Sampling Frequency
parts:
Hi,

Vincent, could you confirm that the publication you were referencing here is this now published article?: https://journals.humankinetics.com/view/journals/jmpb/7/1/article-jmpb.2024-0003.xml

If so, it looks like the modified 'autocalibration' function (and associated `g.downsample`) in the publication github repo should perform the type of downsampling originally asked about. Although as far as I can tell, these methods were not applied in the final analyses. Best,

Tom
